title: Learn to Separate the Problem From the Symptom
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership piece argues that leaders routinely mistake the symptoms of a challenge for the problem itself and so address the wrong issue. It uses the image of cutting the top off a weed while leaving the root to regrow. The author explains that the natural tactical question, what should we do about this, tends to surface symptoms rather than causes, and that mislabeling symptoms as problems is the rule rather than the exception. The central move is to replace that question with two diagnostic ones: what would we like to see more or less of, which identifies symptoms, and what is impeding progress toward that outcome, which exposes the underlying problem. Fully excavating that obstacle, the piece concludes, is how leaders make lasting headway on recurring issues.
points: Leaders asked for their biggest problem usually describe a symptom, and treating symptoms is likened to cutting off a weed while leaving its root.
The instinctive tactical question of what to do about a problem is itself identified as the source of misdiagnosis.
Common complaints such as weak sales, attrition, team conflict or poor execution are recast as signs of an underlying challenge rather than problems in themselves.
The diagnostic shift is from asking what we want more or less of to asking what is impeding progress toward that outcome, which points at the root cause.
quotes: At the root of any problem is the primary cause that produces a myriad of symptoms. When leaders address the symptoms and not the problem, they miss the mark. This is akin to cutting off the top of a noxious plant but leaving the root to produce the weed all over again.
Leaders naturally examine a problem and ask what they should do about it. This tactical question commonly reveals the symptoms and not the true problem or its causes.

In the desire to alleviate the discomfort of the symptom, leaders misdiagnose what is really in play and often address the wrong issue. Labeling a symptom as the problem is so commonplace that falling prey to this trap is the rule, not the exception.

A symptom is a sign or indication of a root cause, but is not the cause itself. It indicates something is wrong, but does not point a finger at what is causing it to appear. To avoid this misstep, the best leaders ask a very different question to get to the bottom of what is really wrong.
Sales, customers, profits, talent, attrition, team conflict, and weak execution are common answers. These are not problems, but the signs of an underlying challenge worth identifying and resolving.

Fully excavate this obstacle, as it points directly at the underlying cause of the issue. By tackling the root cause and problem, leaders can make significant headway on improving just about any recurring issue. That’s because digging out the root of the weed is the best way to permanently kill it.
